instructions.task: In a chat where a persuader tries to get the other person (the persuadee) to donate to the charity Save the Children, label the single message marked 'Persuader message to tag' with the persuasion strategy or dialogue act it performs. Use the earlier chat only as context to understand what the tagged message is doing; the label is about the tagged message alone.
instructions.guidance: Choose the option that best describes the main function of the tagged message. When a message starts with a short agreement or reaction and then makes a persuasive point, tag the point, not the reaction. A persuasive argument goes to the appeal type it relies on; a plain social move (greeting, thanks, agreement) goes to its dialogue act.

criteria.greeting: Opening social move: says hello or hi, asks how the partner is doing, or tells the partner how the persuader is doing in reply to their 'how are you'.
criteria.acknowledgement: A bare reaction to what the persuadee just said: agreeing, saying yes, okay, I understand, that's true, that's great, sorry to hear that. Use only when the message adds no argument, information or request of its own.
criteria.thank: Thanks the persuadee (for their time, their donation, their willingness or the chat).
criteria.praise-user: Compliments the persuadee personally: calls them generous, kind, a good person, or praises their decision or attitude.
criteria.greeting_closing: Says goodbye or wishes the partner a good day at the end of the chat.
criteria.source-related-inquiry: Asks whether the persuadee is aware of or familiar with the organization, or what they already know about it.
criteria.task-related-inquiry: Asks for the persuadee's opinions, feelings, preferences or wishes about the cause, the charity or the conversation: what they think or feel about an issue, whether they agree with a view the persuader just stated, how they think children could be helped, whether they want more information, what they are unsure about or why they hesitate.
criteria.personal-related-inquiry: Asks about the persuadee's own life and personal history: whether and how often they donate or volunteer, which charities they have supported, whether they have children or family who give, and similar questions about their own experiences.
criteria.credibility-appeal: Tells the persuadee about the charity itself to build trust in it: what the organization is, its mission, the programs and services it runs, where it works, its history, founder, size, transparency, how much of the money reaches the cause, its ratings or reputation. A plain description of what Save the Children does belongs here. This includes replies to the persuadee's questions about the organization, such as how much it raises or who founded it.
criteria.logical-appeal: Uses reasoning to argue that donating is worthwhile: cause-and-effect claims about what the persuadee's money will achieve, comparisons, consequences, moral or practical arguments about why one should help. Not for figures about how much children suffer (emotion-appeal) and not for saying a small amount is enough (foot-in-the-door).
criteria.emotion-appeal: Tries to stir feelings such as sadness, sympathy, guilt or hope about the children: describes their suffering or need, including facts and statistics about children dying, going hungry, being hurt in wars or living in poverty (even when stated matter-of-factly), narrates the hardship or rescue of a particular child or beneficiary, pictures what a gift does for a starving or suffering child, asks the persuadee to imagine a child's situation, or expresses the persuader's own feelings about it.
criteria.personal-story: The persuader tells about their own personal experience: something they did, saw or lived through themselves, such as their own past giving, volunteering or work with the charity.
criteria.foot-in-the-door: Lowers the barrier to giving: suggests a specific small or reduced amount, says that even a tiny sum or a fraction of their earnings helps, or proposes starting small. The point must be that the amount is small; asking for the full reward is not this.
criteria.self-modeling: The persuader states their own intention or action of donating (that they will donate, have donated, or would donate an amount) to set an example.
criteria.donation-information: Explains how the donation works in this task: that it comes from the task payment, the range of amounts allowed, that the researchers will pass it on to the charity, or other procedural details of donating.
criteria.proposition-of-donation: Directly asks or invites the persuadee to donate, or asks whether they would be willing to donate, without asking for a specific amount.
criteria.ask-donation-amount: Neutrally asks how much the persuadee would like or is willing to donate, without suggesting a reduced figure.
criteria.confirm-donation: Confirms, checks or repeats back the donation amount or decision the persuadee has stated.
criteria.practical-reply: Answers a question from the persuadee with logistics or neutral information (e.g. pointing to a website, saying where to find details, answering about themselves) that does not itself argue for the charity or the donation.
criteria.off-task: Talk about a subject unrelated to the charity, children or donating (e.g. where someone lives, unrelated news or history), or remarks about the study itself, such as how many turns are needed to finish.
criteria.other: Any other message that fits none of the options above: small talk and miscellaneous remarks, fragments, unclear or garbled text, filler.

members.name: persuasion_v3b
members.instructions: Below is a chat in which a persuader is trying to convince a persuadee to give money to Save the Children. Which strategy or dialogue act does the final persuader message (the one marked for tagging) carry out? Read the earlier turns only to understand that message. If the message begins with a brief 'yes' or 'I agree' and then argues, informs or asks something, classify what follows rather than the agreement.

criteria.greeting: Hello/hi, asking how the other person is, or saying how the persuader is doing when the persuadee asked.
criteria.acknowledgement: Nothing but a reaction to the persuadee's last turn (agreement, yes, okay, I see, that's nice, sorry about that), with no argument, fact or request added.
criteria.thank: Expresses thanks to the persuadee, e.g. for their time, their gift or their willingness.
criteria.praise-user: Compliments the persuadee as a person or their choice: generous, kind, good-hearted, a great decision.
criteria.greeting_closing: An end-of-chat farewell or good wishes for the rest of the day.
criteria.source-related-inquiry: A question about whether the persuadee is familiar with the organization or what they already know of it.
criteria.task-related-inquiry: A question seeking the persuadee's views: their opinion or feelings on the cause or the charity, whether they share a view the persuader just gave, ideas for helping, whether they want more details, or what makes them hesitate.
criteria.personal-related-inquiry: A question about the persuadee's own life and track record: whether or how often they give to charity or volunteer, which causes they have supported, their family and children.
criteria.credibility-appeal: Information about the organization meant to make it trustworthy: what it is, its aims, the programs it runs and the places it works, its history and founder, how efficiently it uses money, its standing or ratings. This includes replies to the persuadee's questions about the organization, such as how much it raises or who founded it.
criteria.logical-appeal: An argument from reason for giving: what the persuadee's money will accomplish, comparisons, consequences, moral or practical reasons to help. Figures about children's suffering go to emotion-appeal; claims that a small amount suffices go to foot-in-the-door.
criteria.emotion-appeal: Appeals to the persuadee's feelings (sadness, pity, guilt, hope) about the children: describing their suffering or need, including numbers on deaths, hunger, abuse or war, telling the story of a particular child's hardship or rescue, picturing what a gift does for a hungry child, asking the persuadee to imagine, or voicing the persuader's own feelings.
criteria.personal-story: An account of the persuader's own first-hand experience: things they themselves did, saw or went through, such as their own giving, volunteering or work.
criteria.foot-in-the-door: Makes giving feel easy by keeping the ask small: names a small or reduced amount, says even a little or part of the earnings helps, or suggests starting small. Not when the full reward is asked for.
criteria.self-modeling: The persuader says they themselves will give, have given, or would give, setting an example.
criteria.donation-information: Practical details of how giving works in this study: the money comes out of the task payment, the allowed range, the researchers forward it to the charity, how and when it happens.
criteria.proposition-of-donation: Invites or asks the persuadee to give, or whether they are willing to, without naming an amount.
criteria.ask-donation-amount: Asks, without suggesting a lower figure, how much the persuadee wants to give.
criteria.confirm-donation: Checks or restates the amount or decision the persuadee has given.
criteria.practical-reply: Replies to a persuadee's question with neutral or practical information (where to look, a link, facts about the persuader) that is not itself an argument for the charity or for giving.
criteria.off-task: Talks about something unrelated to the charity, children or giving (where people live, unrelated topics), or about the study mechanics such as how many turns remain.
criteria.other: Anything else: small talk, odd remarks, fragments, unclear or garbled text.
